name: Amiloride

lead: Amiloride is a mild diuretic that is sometimes mentioned in water-retention talk as a way to reduce fluid and facial puffiness.

It blocks epithelial sodium channels in the distal kidney tubule, so sodium and water are excreted while potassium is retained. It is normally added to a thiazide diuretic for heart failure or high blood pressure. No study has examined it for facial puffiness or appearance.

paras: It is a prescription tablet, usually paired with a thiazide diuretic in medical use, where it also offsets potassium loss from the other drug.

The label's boxed warning says high potassium can be fatal if uncorrected, with roughly 10 percent incidence when used without another diuretic and higher risk with kidney disease, diabetes and older age. Minor nausea and abdominal symptoms are common. It is prescription-only.

chain: Mild diuretic removes sodium and water
angle.text: Amiloride is a mild potassium-sparing diuretic used with other diuretics, and it is sometimes mentioned in water-retention talk for a less puffy face. It blocks sodium channels in the kidney so sodium and water are excreted. No research addresses facial puffiness.

lead: Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that directly blocks epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the distal nephron, producing a mild increase in sodium and water excretion while conserving potassium. It is used mainly alongside thiazide or other potassium-wasting diuretics in heart failure and hypertension. [1][2]

It is listed on the wiki under depuffing because it is a diuretic. No published trial has tested amiloride for facial puffiness or any appearance outcome, and no community discussion of it was available to document.
Its US label carries a boxed warning on hyperkalemia, reported in about 10 percent of patients when amiloride is used without a potassium-wasting diuretic. [2]

paras: The US label indicates amiloride as adjunctive treatment with thiazide or other kaliuretic diuretics in congestive heart failure or hypertension, to restore normal potassium or prevent hypokalemia. [2] Grokipedia notes its diuretic and antihypertensive effects are weaker than those of thiazides, so it is used as an adjunct. [1]

The epithelial sodium channel that amiloride blocks was cloned in 1994 and is made of three homologous subunits; it carries the rate-limiting step of sodium reabsorption in the distal renal tubule, colon, and some exocrine ducts and lung. [3] Gain-of-function mutations in the channel cause Liddle's syndrome, a heritable form of hypertension. [4] Amiloride has also been used as a research tool for ion transport. [5]

The label states that amiloride is usually well tolerated apart from hyperkalemia, which if uncorrected is potentially fatal and is more likely with renal impairment, diabetes and older age. [2] Minor reactions such as nausea, abdominal pain and flatulence were reported in about 20 percent of patients, with frequency similar to hydrochlorothiazide groups. [2] Animal studies at high multiples of the human dose found no fetal harm, though the drug crossed the placenta. [2]

No studies found on amiloride for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing. Registered trials concern resistant hypertension, proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis and migraine aura, among others. [6][7]

timeline.event: Amiloride-sensitive epithelial sodium channel subunits identified; Liddle's syndrome linked to channel mutations. [3][4]
